strategy: A planning relationship should make it easier to decide what to do, when to do it, and who is responsible. Ask for the actual deliverables: the analysis, assumptions, action list, decision deadlines, and implementation responsibilities. A conversation about possible strategies is a different deliverable from a written recommendation evaluated against your records.

Compare the engagement over the period you expect to use it. Include required renewal, additional implementation work, return preparation, amendments, and any specialist projects. Two proposals with similar starting prices can cover different work. Ask both firms to identify the first milestone and the point at which the initial engagement is considered complete.
realestate: A useful real estate engagement connects property records to the owner’s broader tax picture. Prepare an entity chart, property list, acquisition and service dates, current depreciation schedules, operating reports, and anticipated transactions. Then ask what the adviser will analyze and what must be obtained from other professionals. Several properties held in separate entities can require more coordination than a single property.

Compare the proposed scope for bookkeeping, entity returns, personal planning, study coordination, and transaction advice. If a property study is involved, ask who evaluates its potential use within your overall tax position. A study estimate alone does not resolve every owner-level question. Make sure each proposal identifies the property and tax year being analyzed.
business: An operating business needs usable records before its owner can make informed tax decisions. Ask whether the engagement starts with books that are already current or includes cleanup. Prepare a year-to-date profit-and-loss statement, balance sheet, entity chart, payroll information, and major planned transactions. The proposal should explain how business results will be connected with the owner’s household forecast.

Recurring bookkeeping, payroll, tax preparation, and a written planning engagement serve different purposes. Compare the work you actually need rather than assuming that any accounting package includes all four. Ask which meetings result in updated projections and which implementation steps remain with your payroll provider, attorney, bookkeeper, or return preparer.
costseg: Technical study scope and tax implementation

Start by separating the property analysis from the wider advisory project. Request the study methodology, evidence requirements, professional review process, deliverable format, and support terms. Ask how the final report will reconcile with the existing asset records. A proposal should identify the property, required inputs, expected delivery process, and the tasks assigned to the return preparer.

A study can be one part of a broader planning engagement. Compare whether each quote covers the property report, reporting coordination, additional specialist work, or owner-level analysis. If you already have a CPA, include that professional in the discussion before ordering the study. Resolve the handoff and responsibility for tax reporting before relying on a preliminary estimate.
software: Digital workflow, review, and CPA acceptance

Convenience is useful when the inputs and deliverable fit the project. Before purchasing an online product, ask what information you must supply, how exceptions are handled, what professional review occurs, and whether the output is an estimate, educational analysis, or final study. Have your return preparer assess the proposed deliverable and the information needed to implement it.

Compare the complete workflow rather than delivery speed alone. A property with renovation history, incomplete records, or unusual features may require additional analysis. Ask what support is available when the preparer has questions and who evaluates the broader owner-level tax position. A digital report and a personalized tax-planning engagement can have different scopes and prices.
medical: Professional income, practice ownership, and personal planning

Medical professionals can have several income arrangements at once. Prepare employment documents, independent-contracting records, partnership information, practice financials, existing entity documents, and investment details. Ask which sources of income the engagement covers and how the adviser will coordinate records obtained from the practice, payroll provider, or partnership. A planning proposal should reflect the actual compensation arrangements.

Compare practice accounting and compliance with the personal planning work you need. Ask whether outside investments and rental activity are included, and which implementation tasks require another professional. A useful scope describes the decisions to be analyzed, the information required, the expected deliverables, and who will coordinate those decisions with the relevant filings.
practice: Practice operations and owner-level tax decisions

A therapy or professional practice needs clear records as its staffing, entity structure, and billing model change. Identify whether the immediate problem is bookkeeping, payroll coordination, entity compliance, or personal tax planning. Prepare current financials and describe planned growth. An industry-focused accounting relationship can provide operational context, while an additional planning project may address a specific owner decision.

Ask each firm to define what happens when the practice changes. Adding contractors, employees, another location, or a second entity can affect the work required. Compare the proposal for the practice with the proposal for the owner’s personal tax position. Establish how the bookkeeper, payroll provider, and preparer will receive and implement recommendations.
wealth: Tax scope inside a wealth relationship

Wealth management can connect investments, retirement, estate work, and tax decisions. The comparison should begin with your actual objective: ongoing wealth management, tax filing, or a discrete planning question. Ask how services are bundled and whether a tax project can be evaluated separately. Record the fees associated with each service and whether changing providers requires moving or reconnecting accounts.

If you already have financial and legal advisers, ask how the tax professional will coordinate with them. Compare the planning deliverables, review process, ongoing access, and renewal terms. A membership or broader wealth relationship can cover different work from a focused tax engagement; evaluate the complete scope instead of comparing only the advertised starting price.
legal: An entity or asset-protection decision often requires coordination between legal and tax professionals. Ask which legal documents are prepared, which tax consequences are analyzed, and who handles ongoing administration. Prepare the existing entity chart, ownership documents, relevant contracts, and tax returns. The engagement should identify the professionals responsible for each part of the proposed structure.

Compare the legal project separately from planning, bookkeeping, and filing work. A proposed entity should have a clear purpose and a practical operating plan. Ask who will implement the structure, what records must be maintained, and whether the tax recommendations are documented. Include legal and ongoing compliance costs when evaluating the overall engagement.
resolution: Immediate tax matters and future planning

Start with any outstanding filing, payment, or notice deadlines. Prepare the notices, relevant returns, account history, and correspondence before discussing a resolution engagement. Ask exactly what representation is included and whether the professional will handle communication for the identified matter. Forward-looking planning can be coordinated with this work, but the scope should make each responsibility clear.

Compare resolution fees and ongoing planning fees separately. Ask what immediate work must be completed before broader recommendations can be made. A useful proposal distinguishes the current matter, required compliance work, and future planning deliverables. Confirm which professional will coordinate information so that advice for future years takes account of the current situation.
filing: Return preparation versus a future planning project

Return preparation starts with information for a particular tax year. A future planning engagement asks how upcoming decisions may affect later results. Describe both needs before requesting a quote. Provide the returns to be prepared, the number of entities, state filing requirements, and any anticipated transactions. Ask whether the quoted consultation addresses those future decisions in detail.

Compare a preparation quote with other preparation quotes and a planning proposal with other planning proposals. If you need both, request a combined view showing separate deliverables and fees. Ask how recommendations will be documented and communicated to the preparer. Establish whether questions after filing or new transactions require another engagement.
solopreneur: An integrated back-office membership can simplify a solo business owner’s recurring tasks. Compare the services needed today with those you expect after growth: entity administration, bookkeeping, payroll, filing, and personal planning. Ask how the membership handles activities outside the core business and whether an additional entity, rental, or unusual transaction needs separate support.

A membership and a focused planning engagement can work together when their responsibilities are clear. Ask who maintains the books, who implements business changes, and who prepares the returns. Include all required recurring fees when comparing proposals. Make sure the proposed planning work uses the same financial records and assumptions as the ongoing accounting service.
books: Reliable records and a usable planning handoff

Clean accounting records help advisers evaluate business decisions with better information. Ask which reports are delivered, how frequently accounts are reconciled, and whether historical cleanup is necessary. Describe the tax decision you want to make so the accounting team can identify the relevant records. A planning project should specify when those records need to be available.

Compare recurring accounting work with the additional advisory work your decision requires. Confirm who handles tax preparation, which meetings address future decisions, and how recommendations reach the person responsible for filings. Establish a shared calendar for record delivery and planning milestones so that accounting work supports decisions before their deadlines.
startup: A startup’s tax obligations and its founders’ personal decisions require different records and analyses. Identify the company filings, accounting deliverables, financing events, and founder transactions that need attention. Ask whether the proposal covers the corporation alone or includes individually scoped owner advice. A company-level engagement should not be assumed to cover every founder’s personal circumstances.

Compare the finance and compliance services required by the company with any separate personal planning project. Ask how information will move between the company team and the founder’s adviser. If a specialized transaction or credit project is needed, request its deliverables and fees separately. Keep the company’s filing obligations and the founder’s planning decisions visible on one coordinated timetable.
digital: Platform records and business tax planning

Online businesses can receive information from several sales, payment, and accounting systems. Identify the records that explain revenue, fees, refunds, inventory if applicable, and payroll. Ask whether cleanup or platform reconciliation is included before planning starts. The adviser should work from a coherent financial picture rather than isolated dashboard totals.

Compare operational accounting services with personalized planning deliverables. Ask what state or jurisdiction information is required and whether the relevant review is included in the proposal. Establish how platform reports will reach the bookkeeper and tax preparer. If your business model is changing, describe that change before the initial forecast is prepared.
fitness: A fitness business needs a clear view of membership revenue, staffing, facility costs, and expansion commitments. Prepare the operating results for each location and describe any planned acquisition or new lease. Ask which advisory work addresses the operating business and which addresses the owner’s separate investments or real estate. Those questions can require coordinated but distinct deliverables.

Compare recurring financial support, cash-management advice, and tax planning separately. Ask how a new location or facility purchase changes the engagement. The proposal should identify who updates the operating forecast and who incorporates it into tax recommendations. Align planning milestones with the actual expansion timetable so that advice can inform the decision.
inventory: A product business needs financial records that reflect inventory movements, supplier arrangements, and distributor deductions. Before asking for a planning model, identify whether the accounting records reconcile those items consistently. Explain any major purchasing or distribution changes. Ask what accounting cleanup is required and which reports the tax adviser will receive.

Compare the recurring accounting scope with the additional planning deliverables. Ask who coordinates inventory information with the preparer and when reliable year-end estimates will be available. A proposal for business bookkeeping can address different work from a personal owner planning engagement. Make the connection explicit so both teams use consistent financial information.
creative: A creative business can change its cash position by changing pricing, staffing, and service mix. Prepare current financials and the operating assumptions behind your next growth phase. Ask how the advisory team will reflect those assumptions in its forecasts. Owner-level planning should be evaluated against the expected business results rather than an outdated revenue target.

Compare business-model advisory work, recurring accounting, and tax planning as separate deliverables. Ask who maintains the forecast and what triggers another review. If you have an existing bookkeeper or preparer, establish how recommendations will be communicated. Tie the planning calendar to hiring, contract, or expansion decisions you expect to make.
regulated: Specialized compliance and a focused tax scope

Some businesses need industry-specific accounting, compliance, or assurance work alongside tax advice. Identify those requirements before comparing firms. Ask which services need specialized professionals and which can be addressed through a focused planning engagement. Prepare the relevant financial reports, regulatory context, and entity structure so each provider can quote the actual project.

Compare specialized audit or compliance services separately from general tax planning. A firm offering a focused owner plan should be evaluated for that scope; a broader professional-services provider may serve additional needs. Ask how specialist findings will reach the tax adviser and who will coordinate implementation. Clarify any required additional engagements before choosing a provider.
national: Focused owner planning or a broader tax relationship

A large tax practice may offer several specialist teams and engagement types. Compare the particular team and proposal you would hire, rather than drawing conclusions from the overall brand. Describe the business, jurisdictions, ownership structure, and personal planning needs. Ask which issues require specialists, which can be handled by the core team, and how work is coordinated.

A focused planning engagement and a broad recurring tax relationship can have different purposes. Request separate scopes for company compliance, individual owner analysis, transaction work, and any required specialist projects. Compare the actual deliverables and total fees over the same period. There is no basis to assume a large firm is automatically more expensive or less responsive; obtain a proposal for your facts.
